pharm: Beta-1 selective adrenergic blocker with nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilatory activity
quick: HTN: 5 mg once daily; titrate at 2-week intervals up to 40 mg/day
Severe (CrCl <30): start 2.5 mg/day; not studied in dialysis
Limit; may add to hypotensive/dizziness effects
BP, heart rate, blood glucose in diabetics, signs of HF
summary: Nebivolol is a beta-adrenergic blocking agent used to treat hypertension and lower blood pressure. At doses up to 10 mg in extensive metabolizers (most patients) it is preferentially beta-1 selective; at higher doses or in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers it also blocks beta-2 receptors. Its antihypertensive mechanism is not fully established and may involve reduced heart rate and contractility, decreased sympathetic outflow, renin suppression, and vasodilation with reduced peripheral vascular resistance. It lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Like other beta-blockers it must not be stopped abruptly, can mask hypoglycemia and hyperthyroidism, and is contraindicated in severe bradycardia, high-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, and severe hepatic impairment.
indications: Hypertension (alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents) to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of fatal and nonfatal cardiovascular events, primarily strokes and myocardial infarctions

dosage.d: Initial 5 mg once daily (monotherapy or combination); may increase up to 40 mg/day
dosage.t: Titrate at 2-week intervals; more frequent dosing is unlikely to add benefit
dosage.n: Individualize to the patient and monitor during up-titration; can be taken with or without food

dosage.c: Hypertension with severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min)
dosage.n: Not studied in patients receiving dialysis
Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >B); not studied in that population

dosage.d: Standard dosing; no age-based dose adjustment necessary
dosage.n: No overall differences in efficacy or adverse events versus younger patients

dosage.d: Standard dosing; no dose adjustment necessary
dosage.n: Clinical effect and safety similar to extensive metabolizers; exposure to d-nebivolol is higher but metabolites contribute to activity

admin: Take regularly and continuously as directed, with or without food
Do not interrupt or abruptly discontinue; when stopping, taper over 1 to 2 weeks when possible
Reduce dose if co-administered with a CYP2D6 inhibitor based on blood pressure response
In known or suspected pheochromocytoma, initiate an alpha-blocker before starting any beta-blocker
Patients should know how they react to the drug before driving or operating machinery
moa: Nebivolol is a beta-adrenergic receptor blocking agent that, in extensive metabolizers (most of the population) and at doses 10 mg or less, is preferentially beta-1 selective; in poor metabolizers and at higher doses it inhibits both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. It lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic and membrane-stabilizing activity and shows no alpha-1 blockade at clinically relevant doses. The active d-nebivolol isomer (beta-receptor affinity over 1,000-fold higher than l-nebivolol) and its metabolites mediate beta-blockade. The antihypertensive response has not been definitively established but may involve decreased heart rate, decreased myocardial contractility, reduced tonic sympathetic outflow from cerebral vasomotor centers, suppression of renin activity, and vasodilation with decreased peripheral vascular resistance.

absolute: Heart block greater than first degree (without a functioning pacemaker)
Sick sinus syndrome (unless a permanent pacemaker is in place)
Hypersensitivity to any component of the product
relative: Bronchospastic disease (in general, patients with bronchospastic disease should not receive beta-blockers)
Diabetes mellitus or fasting/vomiting patients (may mask hypoglycemia and prolong it)
Peripheral vascular disease (may precipitate or aggravate arterial insufficiency)
Thyrotoxicosis (may mask tachycardia; abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm)
Concomitant verapamil- or diltiazem-type calcium channel blockers (additive negative inotropic/chronotropic effects)
History of severe anaphylactic reactions (may be more reactive and less responsive to epinephrine)
monitor: Heart rate and blood pressure (especially with diltiazem/verapamil or digitalis)
Signs of worsening heart failure (weight gain, dyspnea)
Blood glucose and hypoglycemia awareness in diabetic patients
ECG and BP when given with non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Respiratory status in patients with airway disease

preg: Available data in pregnant women are insufficient to determine drug-associated risk of adverse developmental outcomes; there is no boxed warning. Poorly controlled hypertension in pregnancy itself raises maternal risk (pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, premature delivery, delivery complications) and fetal risk (intrauterine growth restriction and death). Beta-blocker use in the third trimester may cause neonatal hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycemia, and respiratory depression; observe newborns and manage accordingly. In rats, nebivolol produced embryofetal and perinatal lethality at doses near the maximum recommended human dose. The U.S. background risk of major birth defects is 2-4% and miscarriage 15-20%.
lact: Breastfeeding is not recommended. There is no information on nebivolol in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production; nebivolol is present in rat milk. Because of the potential for beta-blockers to cause serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, especially bradycardia, nebivolol is not recommended during nursing.
renal: In severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) the recommended initial dose is 2.5 mg once daily, titrated up slowly if needed; apparent clearance is reduced about 53% in this group. Clearance is unchanged in mild impairment (CrCl 50-80 mL/min) and reduced only negligibly in moderate impairment (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). Nebivolol has not been studied in patients receiving dialysis.
hepatic: In moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B), the recommended initial dose is 2.5 mg once daily, titrated up slowly if needed; d-nebivolol peak concentration rises about 3-fold, AUC about 10-fold, and apparent clearance falls about 86%. Nebivolol is contraindicated in and has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >B).

major: CYP2D6 inhibitors (quinidine, propafenone, fluoxetine, paroxetine) increase nebivolol levels - use caution and reduce dose as needed
Verapamil- or diltiazem-type calcium channel blockers (excessive reduction in heart rate, BP, and contractility; monitor ECG and BP)
Catecholamine-depleting drugs such as reserpine or guanethidine (excessive reduction of sympathetic activity)
moderate: Clonidine (discontinue nebivolol several days before gradually tapering clonidine)
Digitalis glycosides (additive slowing of AV conduction and heart rate; increased bradycardia risk)
Disopyramide and other antiarrhythmics/myocardial depressants (additive AV conduction effects)
Myocardial-depressant anesthetics (e.g., ether, cyclopropane, trichloroethylene) - monitor closely perioperatively
minor: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction with digoxin, warfarin, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, spironolactone, ramipril, or losartan
interactions.food: Food does not alter the pharmacokinetics of nebivolol; it may be administered without regard to meals.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may add to blood-pressure-lowering and dizziness; advise caution.
interactions.diagnostics: In controlled trials nebivolol was associated with increases in BUN, uric acid, and triglycerides and decreases in HDL cholesterol and platelet count. May mask tachycardia that signals hypoglycemia or hyperthyroidism.

rare: Abnormal hepatic function (raised AST, ALT, bilirubin)

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate, especially during up-titration
Signs and symptoms of worsening heart failure (weight gain, shortness of breath)
Blood glucose and hypoglycemia awareness in diabetic or fasting patients
ECG and BP when used with diltiazem/verapamil-type calcium channel blockers or digitalis
Hepatic and renal function as clinically indicated
counsel: Do not suddenly stop taking nebivolol - chest pain or a heart attack could occur; the dose will be lowered slowly if stopping
Take it every day exactly as directed, with or without food
Report difficulty breathing or signs of worsening heart failure such as weight gain or increasing shortness of breath
If you have diabetes, know that this drug can mask warning signs of low blood sugar such as a fast heartbeat
If you feel dizzy, sit or lie down and tell your doctor
Tell your doctor before any surgery or anesthesia, and report all other medicines you take
pk: Antihypertensive effect develops over days of dosing; titrate at 2-week intervals
Mean peak plasma concentrations approximately 1.5 to 4 hours after dosing
Effective half-life of d-nebivolol ~12 h in CYP2D6 extensive metabolizers, ~19 h in poor metabolizers
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in tight, light-resistant container
pearls: Beta-1 selectivity is dose-dependent: preferential at doses up to 10 mg in extensive metabolizers, lost at higher doses or in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers
No dose adjustment is needed for CYP2D6 poor metabolizers despite higher d-nebivolol exposure, because active metabolites contribute to beta-blockade
Never stop abruptly in coronary artery disease - risk of angina exacerbation, MI, and ventricular arrhythmias; taper over 1-2 weeks
Continue perioperatively when already on therapy; abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal raises perioperative MI and chest pain risk
Co-administration with verapamil/diltiazem warrants ECG and BP monitoring due to additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects
In pheochromocytoma, give an alpha-blocker before any beta-blocker to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is close to the time of the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: The most common signs are bradycardia and hypotension; other reported effects include cardiac failure, dizziness, hypoglycemia, fatigue, vomiting, and, with beta-blockers generally, bronchospasm and heart block. Because of extensive plasma protein binding (~98%), hemodialysis is not expected to enhance clearance. Provide general supportive and symptomatic care and stop nebivolol when warranted: IV atropine for bradycardia (then isoproterenol or pacing if needed); IV fluids and vasopressors, with IV glucagon possibly useful, for hypotension; isoproterenol or pacing for heart block; digitalis and diuretics (plus inotropes/vasodilators) for heart failure; inhaled beta-2 agonist and/or aminophylline for bronchospasm; IV glucose (repeated, with glucagon if needed) for hypoglycemia. Call the Poison Control Center (800-222-1222).
